lines.text: Every barrel a refinery processes is decided by an optimisation solver: which crudes to buy, how to blend them, when to run each unit.
In India, those solvers are foreign, closed, and licensed by the seat.
So we built one. This is NIRNAY.
Here's a refinery plan built from public Indian data: MRPL-sized distillation units, BS-VI fuel specifications, this year's prices.
Press solve.
The dual simplex drives the infeasibility to zero, and the plan is optimal in milliseconds: the crude slate, what to make, and what every extra unit of capacity is worth.
Then we ask HiGHS, an independent solver, to check. Same answer.
Real plans are whole decisions: how many crude parcels each month, which mode the cracker runs in.
Branch-and-bound closes the gap between the best plan found and the best still possible, and proves that nothing better exists.
This one is a published refinery benchmark: tankers, storage tanks, charging tanks and the distillation unit.
NIRNAY reproduces the published optimum exactly, and draws the schedule.
For very large models, there's a GPU engine.
One and a half million nonzeros, solved in about a second on a laptop graphics card. The same laptop running HiGHS takes over four minutes.
Under the hood, there are three LP engines, chosen by the shape of the problem.
The dual simplex, for exact answers and the warm starts that branch-and-bound needs. An interior-point method, for large sparse models. And PDLP, when a model is big enough for the GPU to pay off.
Branch-and-bound and a quadratic solver sit on top. And every factorisation underneath, the sparse LU, the Cholesky, the LDL-transpose, we wrote ourselves.
None of this is a projection.

Ninety of ninety classic LPs. Thirty-three MIPLIB problems proven optimal, with no wrong answers. A hundred and twenty-one of a hundred and thirty-eight quadratic programs. Every result re-checked by an independent solver.
Checking that carefully even caught mistakes in the reference solvers themselves.
We're slower than HiGHS today, and we say so.
And there's no solver library inside. Every factorisation, every pivot, is our own code.
Next, we close the speed gap: hyper-sparse linear algebra and a better LU factorisation, more cutting planes for the hardest integer problems, and a live MRPL planning model at the finale.
For MRPL, it means planning software it owns. No per-seat licence. Code it can audit. And shadow prices its planners can trust.
NIRNAY. Built for Smart India Hackathon twenty twenty-six, by Team ZeroCloud. The code is open.
